tagline.text: A mountain hot spring in Laguna with natural pools and a hidden waterfall inside a tropical rainforest

location.label: Location
location.text: Calauan, Laguna (entrance on the Alaminos side), between Mount Makiling and Mount Banahaw

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱2,200–4,000 (per person for entrance, or for a tour from Manila)

children.text: Hidden Valley Springs is a natural hot spring in Calauan, Laguna, set in about 110 acres of tropical rainforest between Mount Makiling and Mount Banahaw. It has 6 natural pools fed by hot and cold springs and a hidden waterfall at the end of a forest trail, and it is about 1.5 hours by car from Manila, so it makes a good day out.
Hidden Valley Springs is a natural hot spring resort in Calauan, Laguna, about
75 km

south of Manila. Its entrance is on the Alaminos side, and it sits inside a private estate of tropical rainforest of about 110 acres between Mount Makiling and Mount Banahaw. Unlike the urban-style hot spring resorts of Pansol in Calamba, its main draw is soaking in natural water among old forest and ravines.

It is described as lying inside an old volcanic crater, and according to its promotional material the owners blocked farming and development even during the logging boom of the 1970s, so the forest was preserved. One resort profile says the Roxas family has owned the land since 1918, but part of this history is the resort's own account without independent confirmation, so read it as background only.

Day entrance includes pool use, lunch and an afternoon snack, and the pools are described as 6 natural hot spring pools, 2 kids' pools and 1 natural jacuzzi. The best-known pools are the Soda Pool (water with dissolved carbon dioxide) and the more secluded Lovers Pool, and a forest walk of about
9 minutes
leads to Hidden Falls. Water temperature varies by pool, from cold pools to warm ones that one information site puts at about

(not an official measurement, and some say the pools have cooled slightly in recent years). It also helps to think in advance about who this place suits. It works well if you want to relax slowly in a quiet forest and take photos, or if you dislike the crowded resort pools of Pansol. It does not suit you if you want play facilities such as slides or videoke, or clean, new rooms. Also factor in the long travel time and the cash-only payment.

Guest numbers are deliberately limited, so it is not crowded, which is an advantage, but some reviews say that the entrance fee is high and the facilities are worn. Overnight stays are not offered at present, as far as is known, so plan it as a one-day trip. Prices and what is open change often, so confirm the latest information when you book.

The pools, divided between hot and cold spring water, are laid out in terraces and linked by wooden boardwalks. Each pool has a different temperature, so you can move from one to the next, warming up and cooling down.

It is known as a pool whose water contains dissolved carbon dioxide, so small bubbles cling to your skin. Reviews can make it confusing which pool carries this name, so ask for directions when you enter.
It is quieter than the other pools and surrounded by forest, which makes it a good place to rest peacefully. If you avoid the busy lunch hour, you can enjoy it with much more calm.
About
9 minutes

down a forest trail from the pools you reach the waterfall. Swimming under the falls is not allowed and you may only dip your feet, and at the end of the trail it is safer to follow the staff's guidance.
Centuries-old amlang trees and rainforest paths stretch on. Walking among birdsong and the sound of the stream, it is hard to believe you are less than two hours from Manila.

You can loosen your shoulders and back in the natural jacuzzi, and 2 separate shallow pools for children mean families with kids can use the place too. If a child finds the hot water too much, let them play in the kids' pool.
Day entrance includes a Filipino home-style buffet lunch and an afternoon snack. Reviews are mixed on the food and service, so it is better not to set expectations too high.

items.title: Day course from Manila
items.subtitle: Leave in the morning, return in the afternoon

children.text: From Manila take SLEX, exit at Calamba and follow the Calamba–Tagaytay road, looking for the signs toward Calauan. On weekends, leave early.
Arrive at opening time, check in, pay in cash and get a locker assigned.
First look around the quiet pools, then start with the cooler pools. Check the temperature of each pool with your hand first.
Alternate between the cold and warm pools and compare how your body feels. If you start to feel cold, move straight to a warm pool.
Walk the forest trail with a staff member to Hidden Falls. The trail is slippery, so wear water shoes.
Have the lunch buffet at the open-air pavilion restaurant.
Rest by alternating between the Soda Pool and the Lovers Pool.
Have the afternoon snack, shower and leave. For tour packages the target arrival back is usually 17:30, so in practice you leave the resort earlier than that.
Opening hours differ by source. One information site lists 06:00–18:00, while the official site only says it is open for day tours every day. Confirm arrival and departure times when you book.

The resort is in the hills and more than 5 km from the nearest stop, so allow plenty of time.

The springs can be enjoyed in any season, but the forest and waterfall trails become slippery when it rains, so the November–April dry season is the most comfortable. March–April days are hot, so the cold pools feel more refreshing, while on December–February mornings it is cool and the warm pools are especially good.

During the June–October rainy season, afternoon showers and typhoons are frequent, the forest paths are wet and the waterfall trail is more dangerous. Soaking in the rain has its charm, but getting around is awkward, so bring a raincoat and water shoes. Weekends and holidays can be busy even with limited numbers, so a weekday visit is best.

Overnight stays inside the resort are known not to be offered at present, so plan Hidden Valley Springs as a day trip. It once had log-style bungalow rooms and there is talk of a reopening, but no schedule has been confirmed. If you want to stay longer than a day, it is realistic to book a room in Calamba, in downtown San Pablo or in Los Baños, and travel back and forth.

Lunch and a snack included in the entrance fee are the basics. The resort has three dining areas, including an open bamboo pavilion and an enclosed restaurant, plus a cafe and a souvenir shop. Opinions on the food and service are mixed, so if you are particular, bring some snacks and water of your own. Ask when you book whether outside food is allowed.

After the day is over, it is nice to come into San Pablo and have dinner at a local restaurant. San Pablo is known as a city famous for coconut dishes, and many travelers buy coconut sweets as snacks on the way. Restaurant hours vary by season, so confirm them locally.
Payment is often cash only, and there is no ATM inside the resort. The nearest ATMs are in Alaminos and Calamba, so prepare cash in advance.
Towels are not provided. Bring a towel, a change of clothes and a plastic bag.
A swimsuit is required. Wear water shoes or sandals with good grip for the forest and waterfall trails.
If you arrive early at opening time, you can enjoy the quiet morning hours for longer.
When you go all the way to the waterfall, it is safer to go with a staff member. Swimming under the falls is prohibited.
On a tour, the target is to be back by 17:30, so in practice you leave earlier. Leave some slack in your schedule.
Book by the email or phone number given on the official site, and get the price and inclusions in writing by message.
Because it is a protected forest, stay on the designated paths and take your trash with you.
On rainy days, bring a raincoat, a bag that can get wet and spare socks. Keep your luggage to a minimum.
When you move through several pools, do not step straight from a warm pool into a cold one. Rest for a moment and let your body cool down.
The forest and waterfall trails are very slippery after rain. Swimming under the falls is prohibited, so follow the staff's guidance at the end of the trail.
The entrance fee varies by source, from ₱2,200 to 3,000, so be sure to confirm the latest price when you book. Some reviews also say that the facilities and service are disappointing for the price.
It takes cash only and there is no ATM, so prepare plenty for the entrance fee and transport.
Some visitors say that the water temperature has dropped from what it used to be because of a geothermal power plant, but this is not a confirmed fact.
There is no confirmed information on wheelchair access. The terrain is uneven, so ask in advance about path conditions if you are bringing small children or older people.
Outside food policy, opening hours and whether overnight stays are available may change, so check the latest announcements.
It is a protected forest with wildlife and insects. Bring insect repellent against mosquitoes and spiders, and do not break branches or pick plants.

, which continues along the mountain from Hidden Valley, has tropical forest trails and a spa district, so it pairs well with a hot spring trip.
